added_claim_errors: "the 15-year clock restarts for the new beneficiary" (in the change-beneficiary option) is stated as settled. The key says the reset is unresolved with no IRS guidance. Elsewhere A hedges with "can restart".

"to count for 2026 the money needs to land in the Roth by December 31, 2026" and "a January arrival may count against 2027" treat December as the deadline. A rollover designated for 2026 can run to April 15, 2027, though plans vary.
"If the annual limit rises with inflation, this compresses to four or five years" is wrong or misleading. At $8,000 a year, four years is only $32,000, so it still takes five.
"Most do by 2026, but not all" (plans supporting 529-to-Roth) is unverifiable.
"Several states still don't treat these transfers as a qualified 529 use" is generic, with no states named and nothing checkable.
The Sources list (savingforcollege, lockwealthmanagement) is secondary and unverifiable.
Checked against the IRS 1099-Q instructions page: the Box 4b, code 1 in Box 7 and son-as-recipient details are correct. The answer omits the 6% excess-contribution excise tax on over-transfers.

"The transfer must be completed by December 31, 2026 to count against the 2026 annual limit... if you miss it, it becomes a 2027 rollover" is wrong as a legal deadline. A rollover designated for 2026 can run to April 15, 2027, and plan handling varies. Only "finish by December to be safe" would be fine.

"The 529 plan will issue Form 1099-Q to you as account owner" is wrong. The IRS 1099-Q instructions I opened say the recipient of a QTP-to-Roth trustee-to-trustee transfer is the designated beneficiary (the son).

The state list (30 states follow federal; Indiana, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Utah and Vermont recapture deductions; Colorado, Missouri and New Jersey undecided) comes from one secondary survey (praetorianguard.biz). It is unverifiable and may be stale. California "earnings plus 2.5% penalty" is an acceptable reading, and the key treats whole versus earnings as unresolved.

"If you transfer more than the eligible amount, the excess is a nonqualified withdrawal — tax and 10% penalty on the earnings" is loosely framed around the eligible amount rather than the annual cap. It omits the 6% Roth excise tax.
"He is 22" is an assumption, since he could be 21.
S. 5550 (introduced September 24, 2026, referred to Finance, would eliminate the aggregate limit) checked on govinfo and correct.

reasons: Both answers correct the premise at the start with the $7,500 annual cap, the $35,000 lifetime cap and the $13,000 that can never go, and both give the son-owned Roth, direct-transfer, 5-year and 15-year points. Both miss the 6% excise tax and the full consequences of moving all $48,000 (key point 5, vague), and both state December 31 as the deadline instead of April 15, 2027 (key point 7, wrong). A wins key point 2: it gives the 2026-2030 schedule with $5,000 in 2030, while B only says to repeat yearly. A is penalised for stating "the 15-year clock restarts for the new beneficiary" as settled, which the key treats as a major error, for an inflation line that says the schedule could "compress to four" years, and for much greater length (CPA questions, a repeated trap list, source links). B hedges the 15-year reset with "may", is about half the length, and its only added factual miss is the 1099-Q recipient, which I checked against the IRS instructions and which is wrong. That leaves B ahead by a slight margin.
